title: Between a man and his heart
hookLine: Allah comes between a person and his heart (8:24)
carry: he is nearer than my heart

cards: Pick up an old diary, and the person who wrote it can seem like a stranger: in love with things since dropped, afraid of things that never came, sure of plans that now look foolish. Hearts change.

In Arabic the heart is qalb, and the same root gives the word for turning: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called God muqallib al-qulub, the Turner of hearts. Surah eight has a verse about who stands at that turning point.

teach.h: RESPOND TO WHAT GIVES YOU LIFE.
teach.b: Verse twenty-four opens with an invitation: O you who believe, respond to Allah and the messenger when he calls you to what gives you life.

Then, in Pickthall's words: “know that Allah cometh in between the man and his own heart,” and that to Him you will be gathered. What does that mean? Early commentators gave two readings, and both are still taught.
One: Allah is closer to a person than their own heart. Surah fifty says He is nearer than the vein in their neck. The heart is the most inward thing a person has, and He is nearer still.
Two: Allah can turn a heart. He can stand between a person and what their heart wants, or the faith they assumed they'd always have.
So, the verse implies, respond while your heart is open; don't assume you'll feel the same next year. That second reading sits behind a du'a the Prophet is reported to have said often.
In Tirmidhi's collection, his wife Umm Salamah says it was the du'a he made most: ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik.
O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion.

teach.h: BETWEEN A MAN AND HIS HEART.
teach.b: Asked why, he said every heart is held between two fingers of the Most Merciful, and He turns it as He wills. That's a man whose heart his followers trusted completely, asking for steadiness, every day.
The heart is not a fortress. It's a door on a hinge, and the verse says who holds the hinge.

how: Muslims repeat the Prophet's du'a, ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik (O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion), especially in hard or uncertain times.

a person whose moods change from day to day
the beating heart at the center of the chest

commentators gave only one reading of 8:24
two classic readings: Allah is nearer than the heart, and He can turn the heart.
the Prophet often asked for his heart to be made firm
Umm Salamah reports it as his most frequent du'a (Tirmidhi).

games.q: Umm Salamah hears the Prophet ask, again and again, for a steady heart. what does he answer when she asks why?
o: he was worried about one companion.
every heart is between two fingers of the Most Merciful, who turns it as He wills.
games.why: hearts turn, so he asked for steadiness every day: no heart, even his, was treated as a fortress.

practice: Put a hand on your chest if that feels right, feel the heartbeat or just the warmth, and think of one way your heart has turned lately, toward something good or away from it, without judging it.
If you pray, say the Prophet's du'a slowly, in Arabic or English, O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm; if you don't, rest with the verse's picture of a heart that can turn.
